title: Temporal kernel cancelation and GPU hopping heuristic notes
summary: Notes from exploration of an intermittent latency spike where kernels appear to 'cancel' and subsequent kernels run on different SM groups (GPU hopping). Hypothesis: cuda-graph replay + queue preemption interacts with KV cache placement, causing temporal eviction and L2 thrash.
content:
Background:
Observed an intermittent class of tail-latency spikes (~95-99th percentile) on the microbatching decoder path. Spike pattern: short stall (~3-10ms) mid-decode, then a resumed stream where subsequent kernels execute on a different subset of SMs (based on Nsight capture).

What I ran:
- Captured Nsys (Nsight Systems) timeline for steady load (p90) and for a reproduced spike window.
- Enabled CUDA Graph mode for the batcher when batch_size >= 4; toggled graph replay off/on to compare.
- Instrumented host-side trace points around kv_prefetch, kv_commit, decoder_dispatch.
- Extra run with L2/DRAM counters and sm_efficiency counters (cuda-metrics).

Key observations (from Nsys timelines and metrics):
- Around the spike start there is a short gap where the decoder dispatch kernel emits a launch but the corresponding kernel completes almost instantly (duration < 50us) with a low instruction count. We labelled this temporal cancelation.
- Immediately after, a longer decode kernel launches and completes but shows poor warp efficiency (~55%) and very low SM occupancy relative to baseline.
- The set of SMs active before vs after the event differs: pre-spike SMs 0-22 were hot; post-spike SMs 24-47 show most activity. The timeline shows a gap (~4-7ms) where SM 0-22 go idle.
- L2 read miss ratio increases by ~12% in the post-spike kernels; DRAM bandwidth spikes consistent with cache refills.
- When CUDA Graph replay is disabled, the frequency of these events drops by ~60% (not eliminated).

Hypothesis chain:
1) CUDA Graph replay and our async copy pattern create a scheduling boundary where the runtime enqueues a preemption or high-priority housekeeping kernel (KV maintenance).
2) On certain stream interleavings the small launch (we see low instruction-count 'noop-ish' kernel) is scheduled to the original resident SMs, but the graph replay engine fast-fails it due to an in-flight policy (we see immediate completion with no progress).
3) The runtime then places the subsequent heavier decode kernels on a different scheduling group (GPU hops) to avoid contention with the housekeeping work, but the KV cache lines for active prefixes are still resident on the original SM/L2 region, so the new SM group suffers L2 misses and DRAM refills.
4) The combination of evictions + cross-SM pointer chasing causes observable latency blips and reduced warp efficiency.

Evidence supporting hypothesis:
- Counterfactual run: pinning dispatch to a single stream and disabling graph replay reduces events.
- A synthetic test that does explicit kv_prefetch to distributed SMs (flush+prefetch pattern) reproduces increased L2 misses and similar tail behaviour.
- Timeline shows housekeeping kernels (kv_cleanup) appearing right before the tiny cancelled kernel on the hot SM group.

Remaining unknowns / alternative explanations:
- Could thermal or power-management SM gating explain the SM shift? Unlikely: GPU clocks stable in all captures.
- Driver-level preemption semantics might behave differently across driver versions; we've only tested on drivers A and B.
- Hardware-level inter-SM coherence (NVLINK? NVSHMEM?) -- not used in this cluster.

Quick experimental plan (next runs):
- Reproduce with Nsys capture including kernel stackbacktraces for the cancelled tiny kernel to see if it returns early via device-side checks.
- Run with per-SM L2 placement toggles if available (a/b test) to see sensitivity.
- Add an explicit kv-affinity pass: mark certain tensors as preferred for SM group 0-23 and check effect.
- Try graph replay with a forced stream-fencing between housekeeping and decoding to force ordered execution; measure event frequency.
- Try driver 525 vs 537 to look for changes in preemption behavior.

Micro actions / TODOs:
- [Devon] Add verbose small-kernel backtraces to runtime (deadline: 2024-09-18). Linked PR draft: https://github.com/redwood-inference/serving-runtime/pull/412.
- [Maya] Run Nsys with the backtrace flag on the cluster GPU pool (2024-09-16).

- [SRE] Reserve a node with driver 537 for a controlled run (2024-09-20).

Notes to self (scrappy):
- This is messy: we see signatures of both preemption and cache-eviction. Keep both on the table.
- Look up CUDA Graph internals doc – there is a mention of 'empty node completion' optimization which could match the fast-complete tiny kernel.
- When writing repro, vary sequence length; longer prefixes increase severity (makes sense: more KV touch set).

Potential mitigations if confirmed:
- Prefer stream-affined scheduling for decoder workloads to keep KV hotness (making graph replay respect affinity).
- Introduce a tiny pinned noop kernel that serializes graph replay and housekeeping to avoid interleaving. Measure the cost/regression.
- Adjust KV prefetch windows to be slightly conservative when graph replay is enabled.

Appendix: quick metric snapshots (representative)
- Baseline decode kernel: duration 2.3ms, sm_efficiency 87%, occupancy 68%, L2 miss ratio 8%.
- Post-hop decode kernel: duration 3.9ms, sm_efficiency 54%, occupancy 42%, L2 miss ratio 20%, DRAM BW +120GB/s above baseline.
- Tiny canceled kernel: reported duration 30-50us, instructions executed ~100-300, no DRAM activity.

Questions for the team:
- Has anyone intentionally forced SM-group affinity for kernels before? Any runtime knobs hidden in the serving-runtime scheduler that can pin to GPU logical partitions?
- Should we consider disabling CUDA Graph by default for certain instance types until we have a mitigation?

References and related tickets:
- INF-1872 (investigation ticket)
- PR 412 (runtime instrumentation)
- Confluence draft: gpu-preemption-playbook (internal notes)

End of notes.
